dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper addresses the challenge of assessing banking system stability in emerging and developing economies where reliable, comprehensive financial and market data are often missing or opaque, especially for unlisted banks. It formulates this as a need for a simple, transparent, country-level reverse stress-testing metric that can approximate system-wide resilience to credit shocks using accounting data and a focus on the weakest banks in the system.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: Not addressed in this paper; no quantum computing methods, algorithms, or hardware are discussed.

dimension_3_key_results.text: Applying the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP) metric to about 1,500 banks in 59 EMDEs during COVID-19, the authors find a median country CDBP of 9.8 percentage points, with two countries having Banks at Risk that are already undercapitalized. Regional patterns show substantial dispersion, with Sub-Saharan Africa having the highest median CDBP but wide interquartile range, while South Asia exhibits the lowest median CDBP at 3.8 percentage points. Empirically, the CDBP is only weakly associated with EIU banking risk measures and with standard macro-financial and financial soundness indicators, suggesting that it encapsulates complementary information; robustness checks including profit buffers yield very similar assessments (correlation 0.953).

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The CDBP is compared against traditional macro-financial and financial soundness indicators, as well as the EIU banking risk indicator, and the authors report that these associations are relatively weak and explain little of the variation in CDBP. They interpret this as evidence that the CDBP provides complementary information to standard country-level indicators, and suggest it could be used alongside them rather than as a replacement.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors emphasize that the CDBP is a very rough approximation of systemic banking resilience with several important limitations. Conceptually, it focuses only on credit risk, excluding other key risks such as currency and liquidity risk, contagion and second-round effects, contingent liabilities, bank resolution frameworks, and non-linear distress dependencies among banks. Methodologically, the minimum capital requirement is applied uniformly across banks without bank-specific buffers; the reverse stress test mechanically computes an NPL breakpoint without assigning a likelihood or time horizon; the provisioning rate for new NPLs is fixed and collateral is ignored; and the approach assumes additional provisioning is fully absorbed by capital and effectively excludes profit buffers in its baseline. Data-wise, NPL information is backward-looking, lagged, and may be underreported; the bank sample can be incomplete; COVID-19 policy support measures may have reduced balance-sheet transparency; and the authors stress that the metric should ideally be complemented by richer supervisory data and additional stress tests.

dimension_6_future_work.text: The authors suggest that the CDBP could be developed and used as a basic monitoring tool and as a useful input to form a preliminary view of a banking sector’s resilience, particularly in data-poor EMDEs. They argue it should complement, rather than replace, traditional country-level indicators and be used in conjunction with more detailed stress tests and richer supervisory information. They also propose that high or concerning CDBP signals could trigger more in-depth supervisory risk reviews and targeted analytical work.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The contribution claimed is the development of a simple, transparent, reverse stress-testing based country-level indicator—the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP)—that uses bank-level accounting data to approximate system-wide resilience to credit shocks in EMDEs. The novelty lies in focusing on the tail of the most vulnerable banks that together hold at least 20% of system assets (Banks at Risk), consolidating their balance sheets to derive a systemic breakpoint measure, and demonstrating that this tail-risk-focused indicator provides complementary information to existing aggregate measures.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the paper defines a bank-level Break Point as the NPL ratio at which increased loan-loss provisioning depletes capital buffers above minimum requirements, and then computes a Distance from Break Point (DBP) as the difference between this threshold and the current NPL ratio. It aggregates by selecting the most vulnerable banks (lowest DBP) until they represent at least 20% of system assets, breaking ties by bank size, and consolidates their balance sheets to compute the CDBP. Key modeling assumptions include that incremental provisioning is fully absorbed by capital, a fixed 55% provisioning rate for new NPLs, uniform minimum capital requirements, and ignoring collateral and profits in the base case, with a profit-buffer robustness check. The empirical application uses Fitch balance-sheet data for around 1,500 commercial banks in 59 EMDEs as of Q3 2020, falling back to the latest data not older than 2019 when necessary, and the authors explicitly note potential issues with NPL data lags, underreporting, incomplete bank coverage, and COVID-19 support measures that may obscure true asset quality.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The application during the COVID-19 pandemic is framed within broader macro-fiscal and sovereign risk concerns: the authors note that large projected GDP contractions in some countries could impair bank resilience and that weak banks may contribute to a bank–sovereign doom loop by undermining sovereign debt sustainability.
